prompt: Definition 6.1. What is \(\int_a^b (u(t)+iv(t))\,dt\)?

steps.why: The integral is defined by integrating the real part and the imaginary part separately.

memory: Split \(u+iv\). Integrate each part. Put \(i\) on the second.

prompt: A half period of \(e^{it}\) starts at \(\alpha\), not at \(0\). What is the integral?

steps.answer: \(2ie^{i\alpha}\). It equals \(2i\) only when \(\alpha\) is a multiple of \(2\pi\).
steps.why: The picture half turn starts at 0, so that one is \(2i\). A half period that starts at \(\alpha\) is rotated by \(e^{i\alpha}\).

memory: Any full period of \(e^{it}\) is \(0\). A half period is \(2ie^{i\alpha}\).

prompt: Theorem 6.1. You have a parametrization \(z(t)\). What is \(\int_C f(z)\,dz\)?

steps.answer: \(\int_a^b f(z(t))\,z'(t)\,dt\). Any parametrization of the same contour gives the same value.
steps.why: The contour integral is an ordinary integral of \(f(z(t))z'(t)\) on the real interval.

memory: Replace \(z\) by \(z(t)\) and \(dz\) by \(z'(t)\,dt\).

prompt: Evaluate \(\int_C e^{z}\,dz\), where \(C\) is the segment from \(0\) to \(2+i\pi/4\). What is the parametrization?

steps.why: The segment from \(0\) to \(B\) is \(z(t)=Bt\).

memory: A segment from \(A\) to \(B\) is \(z(t)=A+(B-A)t\) for \(0\le t\le 1\).

prompt: Continue Example 6.7. \(z(t)=(2+i\pi/4)t\).

steps.why: \(z(t)\) is linear, so the derivative is the constant \(2+i\pi/4\).

memory: After multiplying by \(z'(t)\), a segment integral of \(e^{z}\) from \(0\) to \(B\) is \(e^{B}-1\).

prompt: \(C\) is the upper unit semicircle from \(1\) to \(-1\), and the integrand is \(z^{2}\). Which parametrization matches the book's positive direction?

steps.why: The upper semicircle runs from \(1\) through \(i\) to \(-1\), which is \(e^{it}\) for \(t\) from \(0\) to \(\pi\).

memory: The upper unit semicircle is \(e^{it}\) from \(0\) to \(\pi\), and \(dz=ie^{it}\,dt\).

prompt: Continue the semicircle. \(z(t)=e^{it}\), \(dz=ie^{it}\,dt\), and \(f(z)=z^{2}\).

steps.why: \(z^{2}=e^{2it}\) and \(z'=ie^{it}\), so the product is \(ie^{3it}\).

memory: On \(e^{it}\), a power \(z^{n}\) becomes \(e^{int}\), then multiply by \(ie^{it}\).

prompt: A segment.
memory: Compute \((z-a)^{n+1}/(n+1)\) at the two ends when \(n\ne -1\). For \(n=-1\), take the change in argument along the segment.

prompt: Cauchy's proof of Theorem 6.5, as the book gives it on page 184. Assume \(f'\) is continuous and \(C\) is positively oriented.

steps.text: The book writes \(\int_C f(z)\,dz = \int_C (u\,dx - v\,dy) + i\int_C\) ___ .
steps.why: Equation (6.28) splits the integral into those two real line integrals.

steps.text: Green's theorem turns the real part into \(\iint (-v_x - u_y)\,dx\,dy\). The imaginary part becomes \(\iint\) ___ \(dx\,dy\).
steps.why: Green's theorem with \(P=v\) and \(Q=u\) produces \(u_x-v_y\).

steps.text: Cauchy-Riemann says \(u_x=v_y\) and \(u_y=-v_x\), so the integral equals ___ .
steps.why: Both double integrals are integrals of \(0\).

memory: Cauchy's proof: split, apply Green, then Cauchy-Riemann. Both integrands die.

prompt: The same proof. Pick the step the book actually uses.

steps.why: Page 184: Cauchy's proof is the intuitive one, and it needs \(f'\) continuous. Goursat removes that hypothesis.

steps.text: Once both double integrals are zero, you conclude ___ .
choices: the integral equals the length of \(C\)
steps.why: That is the statement of Theorem 6.5.

memory: Reach for Theorem 6.5 when \(f\) is analytic inside and on a simple closed contour. The integral is \(0\).

prompt: The pole sits inside both closed contours, and \(f\) is analytic between them. The two integrals are equal. Which result is that?

choices: Corollary 6.1, so the value is always \(2\pi i\)
steps.why: Theorem 6.5 does not apply: the pole means there is no simply connected domain of analyticity containing the curve. Deformation is the result that keeps the value.

memory: A pole inside is not a reason to quote Theorem 6.5. Quote deformation, then Corollary 6.1 if the integrand is a power of \(1/(z-z_0)\).

prompt: \(C\) is a simple closed contour, positively oriented, and \(z_0\) is inside \(C\). What are \(\int_C dz/(z-z_0)\) and \(\int_C dz/(z-z_0)^n\) for an integer \(n\ne 1\)?

steps.why: Deform to a circle about \(z_0\). The power \(-1\) leaves \(i\int_0^{2\pi} d\theta\). Every other integer power integrates to \(0\).

memory: Inside: \(2\pi i\) only for the power \(-1\). Every other integer power is \(0\).

prompt: A circle.
memory: Look first: is the pole inside, and is the power exactly \(-1\)? That is the only case that is not \(0\).

prompt: Example 6.1. Evaluate \(\int_0^1 (t-i)^3\,dt\) by splitting the real and imaginary parts.

steps.why: \((t-i)^3=(t^3-3t)+i(1-3t^2)\). From 0 to 1 the real integral is \(-5/4\) and the imaginary integral is 0.

memory: Split \(u+iv\), integrate each part, and add them with \(i\) on the second.

prompt: Theorem 6.3, the ML inequality. If \(|f|\le M\) on \(C\) and \(L\) is the length of \(C\), what bounds the integral?

steps.why: Theorem 6.3, page 177. The bound is the length times a bound on the modulus.

memory: Length times a bound: \(|\int_C f\,dz|\le ML\).

prompt: Example 6.14. \(\int_{|z|=2} 2z/(z^2+2)\,dz\). Partial fractions split the integrand into \(1/(z+i\sqrt{2})\) and \(1/(z-i\sqrt{2})\).

steps.text: Both poles lie inside \(|z|=2\), so the integral equals ___ .
steps.why: Corollary 6.1 gives \(2\pi i\) for each pole. The sum is \(4\pi i\).

memory: Each interior simple pole of \(1/(z-z_0)\) contributes \(2\pi i\).

prompt: Example 6.15. The same integrand on \(|z-i|=1\). Which pole is inside that circle?

steps.text: The inside pole is ___ , so the integral is \(2\pi i\).
steps.why: \(i\sqrt{2}\) is inside \(|z-i|=1\). \(-i\sqrt{2}\) is outside, so that term is \(0\) by Theorem 6.5.

memory: A pole outside a simple closed curve contributes \(0\).

prompt: Example 6.16. On the figure-eight contour, \((z-2)/(z^2-z)=2/z-1/(z-1)\).

steps.why: The \(2/z\) term contributes \(-4\pi i\) and the \(1/(z-1)\) term contributes \(-2\pi i\).

memory: On a figure eight, track the orientation of each loop before you quote \(2\pi i\).

prompt: Theorem 6.9. \(f\) is analytic in a simply connected domain, and \(F'=f\). What is the integral from \(z_0\) to \(z_1\)?

steps.why: Theorem 6.9, page 194.

memory: Analytic on a simply connected domain: evaluate the antiderivative at the ends.

prompt: \(C\) joins \(-1-i\) to \(3+i\), and the integrand is \(z\). An antiderivative is \(z^2/2\).
memory: For \(z\), the antiderivative is \(z^2/2\).

prompt: Theorem 6.10. Write \(f(z_0)\) as a contour integral.

steps.answer: \(f(z_0)=\dfrac{1}{2\pi i}\int_C \dfrac{f(z)}{z-z_0}\,dz\), with \(z_0\) inside the positively oriented simple closed curve \(C\).
steps.why: Cauchy's integral formula, page 197.

memory: The value inside is \(1/(2\pi i)\) times the integral of \(f(z)/(z-z_0)\).

prompt: Example 6.21. \(C\) is \(|z|=2\), positively oriented, and \(1\) is inside \(C\).

steps.why: Theorem 6.10 with \(f(z)=e^{z}\) and \(z_0=1\) gives \(2\pi i\, e\).

memory: \(e^{z}\) at \(1\) is \(e\), then multiply by \(2\pi i\).

prompt: Morera's theorem. \(f\) is continuous in a simply connected domain, and \(\int_C f(z)\,dz=0\) for every closed contour in that domain. What follows?

steps.why: Theorem 6.13, page 203, is the converse of Cauchy-Goursat.

memory: Every closed contour integrates to \(0\), and \(f\) is continuous on a simply connected domain: \(f\) is analytic.

prompt: Liouville's theorem. \(f\) is entire and \(|f|\) is bounded on the whole plane. What is \(f\)?

steps.why: Theorem 6.18, page 206. Cauchy's estimate \(|f'|\le M/R\) goes to \(0\) as \(R\) grows.

memory: Bounded and entire means constant.

prompt: \(e^{z}\) is entire. Does Liouville say it is constant?

choices: Yes. Every entire function is constant
steps.why: \(|e^{z}|=e^{x}\) grows with \(x\). Liouville needs a bound on the whole plane.

memory: Entire is not enough. The function also has to be bounded.
